alignment.note: Greek uses imperfect ἐζήτουν (simple past continuous); Peshitta employs periphrastic construction ܘܒܥܝܢ ܗܘܘ (participle + auxiliary 'were seeking'); Vulgate uses imperfect quærebant. All three express ongoing past action, but Syriac makes the durative aspect explicit through periphrasis.

Greek and Vulgate insert coordinating conjunction καὶ / et before the second clause; Peshitta omits the conjunction, proceeding directly to ܘܕܚܠܘ. The Vulgate additionally marks this juncture with a colon, creating a stronger pause than Greek's simple καί.

Greek uses accusative with article τὸν ὄχλον ('the crowd'); Vulgate employs simple accusative turbam without article (Latin lacks definite articles); Peshitta uses prepositional phrase ܡܢ ܥܡܐ ('from the people'), expressing the object of fear with the preposition ܡܢ, a standard Syriac idiom for the source of fear.

Vulgate inserts a second colon after turbam, creating a three-part structure (seeking : fearing : knowing) that differs from the Greek's two-part coordination with γάρ introducing the causal explanation. This punctuation choice reflects Latin rhetorical preference for balanced cola.

Greek uses ὅτι introducing indirect discourse ('that'); Vulgate employs quoniam (causal/declarative); Peshitta uses ܕ- prefix on ܕܥܠܝܗܘܢ, a relative particle construction meaning 'that concerning them.' All three introduce the content of knowledge, but Syriac embeds the prepositional phrase within the subordinate clause structure.

Greek places prepositional phrase πρὸς αὐτοὺς before the object τὴν παραβολήν; Vulgate mirrors this with ad eos before parabolam; Peshitta integrates the prepositional element ܥܠܝܗܘܢ ('concerning them') into the ܕ- clause, creating a more compact construction where word order differs but semantic content remains equivalent.

Greek uses article + noun τὴν παραβολήν; Vulgate employs noun + demonstrative parabolam hanc ('this parable'); Peshitta uses noun + demonstrative ܡܬܠܐ ܗܢܐ, matching Vulgate's word order. The demonstrative hanc/ܗܢܐ adds deictic emphasis absent in the Greek article, making the reference more explicit.

Greek uses aorist participle ἀφέντες with separate pronoun αὐτόν ('having left him'); Vulgate employs ablative absolute relicto eo (perfect passive participle with ablative pronoun); Peshitta uses single verb form ܘܫܒܩܘܗܝ with pronominal suffix, integrating subject and object into one word. All express the same action, but through different participial/verbal strategies.
